action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal MRI for age: no basal ganglia, thalamic or brainstem signal change ('face of the giant panda' absent), normal midbrain morphology, no structural cause
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude a structural, vascular or atypical-parkinsonism cause
action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA, and here also the basal ganglia and brainstem signal change of Wilson disease [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Ceruloplasmin 28 mg/dL, serum copper 88 microg/dL and 24-hour urinary copper 28 microg/24h, all within reference ranges
action_criteria.label: Copper studies to screen for Wilson disease
action_criteria.rationale: Wilson disease is treatable and is screened for in unexplained movement disorders of young adults (EASL 2012: consider it from age 3 to 55) [EASL_Wilson_2012]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Asymmetric reduction of dopamine transporter binding in the left posterior putamen (SBR 1.3, asymmetry index 42%) with relative caudate sparing
action_criteria.label: DaTscan (123I-ioflupane SPECT) if a functional or dystonic tremor is still considered
action_criteria.rationale: The rest tremor with re-emergence, decrement and cogwheel rigidity make the parkinsonism clinically clear; DaT SPECT is indicated only when tremor cannot be clinically separated from parkinsonism, so it is an option here, not a requirement [NICE_NG71]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not dismiss the syndrome as functional or anxiety-related because he is 42: a true rest tremor with re-emergence, decrement on finger tapping and cogwheel rigidity are organic signs of parkinsonism
Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically probable PD (MDS 2015): bradykinesia with rest tremor and rigidity, no absolute exclusion, no red flag; rest tremor is the only supportive criterion at this visit, and the response to levodopa may add a supportive criterion [Postuma_2015]

Screen for Wilson disease (ceruloplasmin, serum copper, 24-hour urinary copper, slit-lamp examination) and record that the normal results and the absence of Kayser-Fleischer rings make it unlikely [EASL_Wilson_2012]

Start symptomatic treatment, since tremor and slowness impair his work: levodopa, a dopamine agonist or an MAO-B inhibitor are all options in young-onset PD; if a dopamine agonist is used, warn about impulse control disorders and excessive daytime sleepiness and ask about them at every visit [NICE_NG71]
Offer genetic counselling, and a PD gene panel if he wishes, because onset is before 50 (PRKN is the commonest recessive cause); a negative panel does not exclude PD
Advise bedroom safety for the dream enactment (he has waved his arm in sleep) and encourage regular aerobic exercise

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, encephalopathy or episodic event; EEG would not change management
No inflammatory, infectious or rapidly progressive feature; CSF has no role in this work-up
No cardiac symptom, sign or murmur
No cardiac indication and no planned drug that needs a baseline ECG
Formal autonomic testing is not part of the PD work-up; bedside orthostatic measurement suffices, and he has no orthostatic symptoms

differential.key_features: Screened for at 42: normal ceruloplasmin (28 mg/dL), serum copper (88 microg/dL) and 24-hour urinary copper (28 microg/24h), no Kayser-Fleischer rings, normal liver tests and no basal ganglia or brainstem signal change on MRI
Onset at 41 without dystonic posturing or diurnal fluctuation; a rest tremor with re-emergence, decrement and dream enactment favour PD

The PCP's 'anxiety and overuse' label is the anchor, but the 4-5 Hz rest tremor re-emerges after a latency, finger tapping decrements, and there is cogwheel rigidity, with no distractibility or entrainment described

differential.diagnosis: Monogenic Parkinson's disease (PRKN, PINK1, LRRK2, GBA1)
differential.key_features: A genetic subtype of PD rather than an alternative; no family history of PD; counselled testing is optional and a negative panel does not exclude it
No exposure to dopamine receptor antagonists, antiemetics or other dopamine-blocking drugs
The tremor is at rest with re-emergence and pill-rolling character, with bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity; none fits essential tremor

key_clinical_evidence: Right-predominant bradykinesia with decrement, cogwheel rigidity and a 4-5 Hz rest tremor with re-emergence over 14 months: parkinsonism
Rest tremor is the only supportive criterion at this visit; no absolute exclusion and no red flag: clinically probable PD [Postuma_2015]

Wilson disease is made unlikely by normal ceruloplasmin (28 mg/dL), serum copper (88 microg/dL) and 24-hour urinary copper (28 microg/24h), no Kayser-Fleischer rings and a normal MRI [EASL_Wilson_2012]
Dream enactment on two occasions and new constipation are non-motor features that fit a synucleinopathy
The 'too young for PD' and 'anxiety and overuse' anchors are the main red herrings; PD with onset before 50 follows the same MDS criteria
In young-onset PD levodopa, a dopamine agonist or an MAO-B inhibitor are all options; agonists carry the ICD warning [NICE_NG71]
Offer counselled testing of a PD gene panel at onset before 50 (PRKN is the commonest recessive cause)

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: PD with onset before 50 is well recognised; a true rest tremor with re-emergence, decrement and cogwheel rigidity are organic signs that a functional or overuse explanation does not account for
red_herrings.data_point: Patient age 42 years; primary care physician attributed tremor to 'anxiety and occupational overuse' prior to neurology referral
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor toward a functional or psychogenic movement disorder or occupational overuse syndrome, delaying recognition of true organic parkinsonism in a young adult

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: An undiagnosed tremor in a relative is non-specific; rest tremor with bradykinesia and rigidity establishes parkinsonism rather than essential tremor
red_herrings.data_point: Maternal uncle with 'tremor of unknown type; never formally diagnosed'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest familial essential tremor and redirect away from Parkinson's disease, or alternatively over-attribute the syndrome to a familial tremor disorder without parkinsonism features

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural and vascular causes on MRI before interpreting a DaTscan [Postuma_2015]

alternatives: Dopamine agonist (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine): impulse control disorders and excessive daytime sleepiness, including sudden sleep onset, are class risks.
MAO-B inhibitor (rasagiline 1 mg daily): avoid with meperidine, tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan and St John's wort.
contraindications: Non-selective MAO inhibitors (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) with levodopa: risk of hypertensive crisis; none prescribed.
interactions: Calcium carbonate antacid: no clinically relevant interaction with carbidopa-levodopa.
general.summary: No interaction of note with the current calcium carbonate antacid. No dopamine-blocking drug on the list.
warnings: Levodopa: nausea is common at initiation (take with food or a small snack); postural hypotension and daytime sleepiness are possible.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Young age and a primary care label of anxiety and overuse push toward a functional diagnosis; the agent must recognise organic parkinsonism and screen for Wilson disease. Two required criteria (MRI and copper studies).
key_educational_points: Young-onset parkinsonism warrants targeted Wilson disease exclusion when clinically appropriate.
Counselled PD genetic-panel testing is optional and a negative result does not exclude the clinical diagnosis.
DaT imaging is optional here because a degenerative-versus-functional/dystonic differential is active; it does not subtype degenerative parkinsonism.
Age alone must not be used to reject a clinical Parkinson disease diagnosis.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Carlos Vega is a 42-year-old right-handed software engineer who presents to the movement disorders clinic accompanied by his wife for evaluation of a progressive right hand tremor and generalized slowness of movement over the past 14 months. He first noticed a subtle intermittent shakiness of his right hand approximately 14 months ago while sitting at his desk and resting his hand on the keyboard. He initially attributed it to overuse and stress. Over subsequent months, the tremor became more persistent, occurring predominantly at rest while watching television or during meetings, and temporarily disappearing when he reached purposefully for an object. His wife noticed the tremor during a family dinner approximately eight months ago, when his hand was resting on the table, and she encouraged him to seek medical attention. He reports progressive right arm stiffness that has affected his work performance — he now makes significantly more typing errors and has slowed considerably at the keyboard. He describes difficulty with right-hand fine motor tasks including handling coins, fastening buttons, and using a screwdriver. He has noticed his right arm does not swing naturally when walking. He reports that his handwriting has become noticeably smaller over the past six months, to the point where his wife and colleagues have commented on it. Over the past four months, he has experienced a pervasive feeling of right-sided fatigue and heaviness that he describes as distinct from muscular tiredness. He has had no frank falls, though he reports feeling mildly unsteady when turning quickly. He notes mild constipation emerging over the past six months requiring increased fiber intake, and occasional episodes of waking from vivid dreams. His wife reports he has acted out a dream on two occasions over the past three months, waving his arm during sleep. He denies visual hallucinations, cognitive changes, dysphagia, or significant orthostatic symptoms. He was seen by his primary care physician three months ago who attributed the tremor to 'anxiety and occupational overuse' and recommended stress management; he was not started on any neurological medications. He denies any exposure to antipsychotics, antiemetics, or other dopamine-blocking agents. He has no prior history of liver disease, psychiatric illness, or toxic exposures. There is no family history of Parkinson's disease or Wilson's disease.

neurological_exam.additional: Handwriting sample shows micrographia with progressive letter compression. Glabellar tap reflex positive (non-habituating). No myoclonus. No alien limb phenomenon. No cortical sensory deficits. No apraxia.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing normal. No intentional tremor. Rapid alternating movements markedly impaired on the right with decrement (bradykinesia); left mildly impaired.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. No Kayser-Fleischer rings noted on slit-lamp biomicroscopy performed at presentation. Facial expression mildly reduced with decreased blink rate. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5. Tongue midline without fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly stooped posture. Reduced right arm swing. Stride length mildly shortened. En bloc turning requiring 4-5 steps for 180-degree turn. Mild hesitancy on gait initiation. Pull test: 1-2 steps retropulsion, self-corrects. No festination. Tandem gait mildly impaired.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. Speech is mildly hypophonic but fluent, grammatically correct, and with intact comprehension, naming, and repetition. MoCA 29/30 (lost 1 point on delayed recall). No evidence of cognitive impairment. Clock drawing normal.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone: cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist and right elbow, accentuated with activation maneuver. Mild lead-pipe rigidity at the right ankle. Left-sided tone normal. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. Bradykinesia is prominent in the right hand — finger tapping shows marked slowing with progressive amplitude decrement. Left hand tapping mildly slow but preserved amplitude. Right foot tapping mildly slow. Resting tremor of the right hand at 4-5 Hz, pill-rolling in character, present at rest and with distraction tasks, suppressed with purposeful movement and re-emerging after a latency. No tremor observed in left hand, chin, or lower extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at bilateral biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, and patellar tendons. Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, temperature, vibration, and proprioception throughout all four extremities. No sensory level.
